newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Highveld Steel shares hit by profit warning.
newsitem.headline: Highveld Steel shares hit by profit warning.

text.p: Shares in South Africa's Highveld Steel and Vanadium Corp Ltd were knocked on Wednesday after the firm warned that its second half profit had been hit by a strike.
The group's shares slumped to equal its year low of 17.00 rand. By 0840 GMt they had recovered slightly to 17.25, down 95 cents or more than five percent.
The firm said a steelworks strike meant that its second half profit come in lower than the first half, despite the fact that it had a full order book with a heavy export load.
But analysts said they were puzzled by the announcement which had taken the market by surprise. They speculated that the firm may have deeper underlying problems.
"It is very difficult to understand. That strike should not effect them like this," said one analyst.
The strike by members of the National Union of Metalworkers of South Africa (Numsa) occurred after a black artisan assistant was allegedly assaulted by a white supervisor.
The dispute, which began on October 22, went to arbitration on November 4 and strikers returned to work a day later.

Analysts said the lost days of production should not be enough to hit the group's profits. They said the firm, most of whose sales are in U.S. dollars and costs in rand, should be reaping the benefits of South Africa's ailing currency.
The rand has lost 30 percent of its value against the dollar since mid-February.
"If they can't get decent growth with the rand the way it is, there must be something else wrong," one analyst said.
On August 6 the company posted first half earnings of 41.5 cents a share, which were themselves sharply down on the previous year's 107.1 cents a share.
A company spokesman said the strike was the major cause of the dip in profit expectations, but conceded there could be some other external factors.
"The majority is the strike," he said.

The spokesman added that steel prices in the period had been low, but that there were now signs they were picking up again. But this would only start to benefit the group in the first quarter of the next financial year, he added.
